These cytokines have the ability to suppress the hematopoietic stem cell from continuing to divide and differentiate into further myeloid stem cells or lymphoid stem cells, right? The issue with that is that now if that hematopoietic stem cell undergoes apoptosis, that thing was supposed to go and make red cells and white cells and platelets. But if you kill it off, now you lose the ability to make red cells, white cells and platelets, and I mean normal ones. So because of that, you can get a decrease in red blood cells, you can get a decrease in platelets, and you can get a decrease in white cells. This collectively, the reduction in all cell lines is called pancytopenia. It's usually an ominous sign that something's going on with the bone marrow potentially. Now, the other sucky thing with MDS is that these dysplastic stem cells, they try to take over as a normal hematopoietic stem cell. It says, ah, I can do it. And what it tries to do is it tries to make red blood cells, but it's not very good. And it has an ineffective, is the terminology we say of making good red blood cells. So you get these like abnormal red blood cells that are usually very large, and you don't make enough of them. And so you get what's called a macrosidic anemia, which is a very common presentation of MDS. Another one is you may have a reduction in effective platelets, which are supposed to help you at a clot. And so these patients can get a thrombocytopenia. And lastly, they may have ineffective leukopoiesis.  vascularitis, inflammation of the blood vessels. So, when we talk about vascularitis, let's first discuss the pathophysiology, and the best way to do this is to cover the three types of vascularitis. The first one is large vessel vascularitis. It's actually not too hard to understand. It's primarily going to affect the aorta and the main aortic branches. So, if you look here, we'll see that they're going to have inflammation of the aorta, inflammation of the branches such as the subclavian, and even the carotids. Now, this inflammation is going to narrow the blood vessels, increase the risk of thrombosis, and sometimes the inflammation can even cause angiosus to form, and we'll talk about that. Now, when we talk about the reason why these large vessels are inflamed, oftentimes we don't have a great reason.
